title: Strategic renewal: exploration & exploitation
summary: Strategic renewal changes the organization’s existing path: its competences, assumptions, activities and relationship with the environment. The lecture contrasts selection pressures with managerial adaptation, and exploitation of existing strengths with exploration of new possibilities.

rows: Selection
Population ecology emphasizes structural inertia; institutional theory emphasizes industry norms; evolutionary views emphasize established routines.
Organizations can become locked into patterns that once worked.
Adaptation
Resource-based, dynamic-capability, behavioral, learning and strategic-choice views allow an active role for management.
Resources, slack, learning and managerial action affect the capacity to renew.
Exploitation
Refine existing competences, routines and fit. Associated with incremental change and single-loop learning.
A competence trap: continued success with existing skills makes alternatives harder to notice.
Exploration
Develop new competences, experiment and challenge assumptions. Associated with unlearning, double-loop learning and more radical change.
A renewal trap: repeated change without consolidation can prevent capabilities from becoming productive.
Internal renewal
New businesses, new products, downsizing and reorganization within the organization.
Can preserve control, but depends on internal resources and willingness to change.
External renewal
Mergers, takeovers, joint ventures and alliances.
Provides access to external capabilities, with integration and coordination demands.

sections.title: Single-loop and double-loop learning
sections.body: Single-loop learning improves action while retaining the governing assumptions. Double-loop learning questions those assumptions: not only whether execution is efficient, but whether the chosen goal or operating logic still makes sense.

sections.title: Renewal is not change for its own sake
sections.body: The lecture treats renewal as a transformation of competences and cognition, an adjustment of alignment, and an alteration of path dependence. An organization can change its chart repeatedly while leaving the underlying strategic assumptions untouched.

steps: Identify what the current strategy exploits successfully.
Look for signals that existing competences are becoming less useful.
Define exploration that tests a new assumption, rather than merely adding activity.
Choose internal or external renewal mechanisms and plan how new learning will be retained.
limits: Selection and adaptation are theoretical lenses. Neither establishes that managers have complete control or that change is impossible. Exploration and exploitation describe different learning needs; neither is universally superior.
recall: How do the competence trap and renewal trap differ?
The competence trap overuses existing strengths and neglects alternatives. The renewal trap keeps changing without consolidating useful capabilities.

title: Organizational flexibility
summary: Flexibility is a response to environmental demands, supported by management capabilities and organizational design. The lecture distinguishes rigid, planned, flexible and chaotic forms. More change is not automatically better: the required flexibility must be compared with the organization’s actual and potential flexibility.

rows: Rigid
Stable, relatively simple and predictable conditions. Strategic programming and routines dominate.
Limited management repertoire; low maneuverability; mechanistic structure and conservative culture.
Planned
More dynamic and complex conditions that remain sufficiently predictable. Planning coordinates a response.
Operational flexibility; a moderate management repertoire and maneuverability.
Flexible
Hypercompetition: dynamic, complex and unpredictable conditions. Adaptation and learning become central.
Operational, structural and strategic flexibility; broad repertoire and high maneuverability; organic, innovative design.
Chaotic
Extremely turbulent conditions. Ad hoc problem solving and spontaneous responses dominate.
Broad repertoire but low maneuverability in the lecture’s summary matrix. A surplus of strategic flexibility need not produce coordinated action.

sections.title: Actual versus potential flexibility
sections.body: Actual flexibility concerns management capabilities: operational flexibility changes the volume or mix of activities; structural flexibility changes how activities are organized; strategic flexibility changes the organization’s direction. Potential flexibility concerns maneuverability created by technology, structure and culture.

sections.title: Run a flexibility audit
sections.body: The lecture compares required flexibility, derived from environmental scanning, with actual management capabilities and potential maneuverability. Gaps inform change trajectories, followed by attention to people, resources, time and evaluation.

steps: Describe the environment’s dynamism, complexity and predictability.
Identify the required operational, structural and strategic responses.
Assess the organization’s current repertoire and maneuverability.
Specify a change trajectory with resources, timing and evaluation criteria.
limits: The four forms are ideal types. An organization may contain different forms across units, and the same form can be appropriate in one environment and unsuitable in another.
recall: Why is a broad management repertoire not enough?
Managers also need organizational maneuverability. Technology, structure and culture can prevent intended responses from being implemented.

title: Renewal paths & the transition dip
summary: Renewal is a transition between organizational forms, not simply a decision to become more flexible. The lecture contrasts routinization with revitalization and illustrates the possibility of a temporary performance decline during transformation.

rows: Routinization
Activities become more established and coordinated; flexibility can narrow as patterns become fixed.
Which routines create reliability, and which now obstruct adaptation?
Revitalization
The organization rebuilds its capacity to respond and renew.
Which management capabilities and design features need to change together?
Transition dip
Performance may initially fall while old arrangements are disrupted and new ones are still developing.
What evidence would distinguish a learning period from a failing transition?
Flexibility audit
Required, actual and potential flexibility are compared before selecting a change trajectory.
Is the problem a lack of managerial repertoire, a lack of maneuverability, or both?

sections.title: Read the J-curve carefully
sections.body: The lecture’s J-curve is a conceptual illustration of an initial decline followed by improvement. It is not a promise of eventual recovery. A transition needs milestones, feedback and a way to revise the approach if the expected capabilities do not develop.

sections.title: Design the journey, not only the destination
sections.body: A target organization may look coherent on paper while the transition creates contradictory demands. Use the flexibility audit to connect environmental needs with changes in capabilities, technology, structure and culture.

steps: Establish the current organizational form and its strengths.
Identify the specific gap that renewal should close.
Sequence changes so that essential activities remain coordinated.
Track learning, capability development and performance through the transition.
limits: The renewal paths and performance curve are conceptual tools. They do not predict the duration or size of a performance dip, and they do not justify continuing a failing change program indefinitely.
recall: What does the transition dip tell a manager to do?
Plan for disruption and monitor whether new capabilities are actually emerging. A dip alone is not evidence that the transformation is working.

title: Organizational ambidexterity
summary: Ambidexterity is the capacity to pursue exploration and exploitation together. The lecture compares structural separation with a context that lets individuals balance both, and introduces four ways of combining different organizational forms.

rows: Structural ambidexterity
Exploration and exploitation are assigned to separate units or groups.
Senior management must coordinate the units and resolve competing demands.
Contextual ambidexterity
People balance exploration and exploitation within their work, supported by the organizational context.
The context must support judgment, initiative and cooperation.
Opposition
Different forms coexist across organizations, such as a flexible orchestrator with planned partners.
Coordination crosses organizational boundaries.
Location
Different forms occupy different organizational locations.
A flexible unit may operate within a more rigid organization.
Synthesis
Features of flexible and planned forms are combined.
Design must make the combination workable rather than merely contradictory.
Temporal separation
An organization shifts emphasis across time.
The ability to switch and retain learning becomes important.

sections.title: Separation does not remove the integration problem
sections.body: Structurally separate units can protect exploration from short-term demands. They also create a need to decide where resources, knowledge and decisions should be shared. Contextual ambidexterity moves more of the balancing task into everyday work.

sections.title: Choose the level at which the tension is handled
sections.body: The lecture’s alternatives locate the tension across organizations, across units, within an organizational design or across time. Make that choice explicit before assigning people conflicting goals.

steps: Specify the exploitation activities that must remain reliable.
Specify what exploration needs protection or discretion.
Choose the level of separation or integration.
Create coordination mechanisms and criteria for resource allocation.
limits: Ambidexterity is not an instruction to divide time equally between two activities. The appropriate balance and design depend on the tasks, time horizons and organizational context.
recall: How do structural and contextual ambidexterity differ?
Structural ambidexterity separates activities into units; contextual ambidexterity enables individuals to balance the demands within their work.

title: Four journeys of strategic renewal
summary: The lecture distinguishes renewal journeys by the exploration or exploitation orientation of top management and of middle/front-line management. Each journey assigns a different role to initiative, integration and industry rules.

rows: Emergent
Top management: exploitation. Middle/front-line management: exploitation.
The market knows best. Limited integration, a holding-company logic, and following industry rules.
Directed
Top management: exploration. Middle/front-line management: exploitation.
Top management knows best. Hierarchical integration guides renewal and adapts industry rules.
Facilitated
Top management: exploitation. Middle/front-line management: exploration.
Middle/front-line management knows best. Loosely connected initiatives are supported and can influence industry rules.
Transformational
Top management: exploration. Middle/front-line management: exploration.
The organization knows best. High integration and tight connections support company-wide renewal and changing industry rules.

sections.title: A vocabulary for who initiates change
sections.body: The matrix helps distinguish renewal led from the top from renewal that emerges through lower-level initiatives. The associated integration patterns explain why the same initiative can develop differently in different organizational settings.

sections.title: Passive and active renewal
sections.body: The lecture also contrasts a more passive response to environmental change with active managerial attempts to shape renewal. This is a question about agency and coordination, not simply whether a company announces a transformation program.

steps: Identify where exploratory initiatives originate.
Assess what top and middle/front-line management are actually doing.
Map the integration mechanisms connecting initiatives.
Check whether that pattern fits the scale and coordination needs of the renewal.
limits: These are ideal-type journeys, not a ranking from bad to good. A company can move between them, and units can exhibit different patterns at the same time.
recall: What separates directed from facilitated renewal?
Directed renewal places exploration primarily at the top; facilitated renewal places it primarily in middle/front-line management.

title: Transactional & transformational leadership
summary: The lecture contrasts leadership based on exchanges, coordination and established expectations with leadership that mobilizes people around changed values, aspirations and direction. The comparison provides a starting point for considering how leadership supports strategic renewal.

rows: Mechanism
Rewards, consequences and agreed exchanges.
Inspiration, enthusiasm and a shared direction.
Orientation
Responding within established arrangements.
Proactively challenging and changing arrangements.
Culture
Working with and developing the existing culture.
Changing the existing culture.
Activity
Planning and execution.
Innovation and renewal.
Motivation
Individual interests in the exchange.
Collective interests and shared purpose.

sections.title: Connect leadership to the renewal task
sections.body: Reliable execution requires clear expectations and coordination. Renewal can also require people to reconsider established assumptions and commit to a different direction. The relevant question is which behaviors the task requires, rather than which label sounds more attractive.

sections.title: Treat the slide as a simplified comparison
sections.body: The original classroom table draws strong contrasts. Actual leaders may combine behaviors, and a settled or turbulent environment does not mechanically determine one correct leadership style.

steps: Identify what needs reliable execution and what needs reconsideration.
Make responsibilities and expectations clear.
Explain the purpose and implications of the proposed change.
Check whether leadership behavior supports both learning and delivery.
limits: The comparison is a teaching device. Charisma alone is not evidence of effective leadership, and transformational language does not establish that a strategy is sound.
recall: How can these leadership approaches support different tasks?
Transactional behaviors clarify exchanges and execution; transformational behaviors can mobilize changes in direction and assumptions. A renewal effort may require both.
